title: Community
hook: a meeting that gets loud, and the Vajjis' conditions for a community that lasts (DN 16)
tomorrow: the tired stranger across from you on the bus. what's their story?

segments.voice: Yesterday, neighbors: the Metta Sutta names the near and the unseen, so the wish lands next door. Today, a whole community in one room, and it's getting loud.

Every group has the meeting. The club, the team, the congregation, the family chat about the holidays. One side says we've always done it this way, and that's why it works. The other says that's exactly why nobody new comes anymore. Voices rise. Someone threatens to quit. The Buddha had a view on what keeps a community alive, and it begins with a king planning a war. In the last journey of the Buddha's life, a king sends a minister to ask whether he can conquer the Vajjis, a confederation of clans.
screen: `THE MEETING THAT GETS LOUD.` → `WE'VE ALWAYS DONE IT THIS WAY.` → `THAT'S WHY NOBODY COMES.` → `A KING ASKS ABOUT THE VAJJIS.`

segments.voice: The Buddha doesn't answer the minister directly. He turns to Ananda and asks: do the Vajjis meet often? Do they meet in harmony, and rise in harmony, and do their business in harmony? Do they keep their old ways, not making new rules or throwing out the established ones? Do they honor their elders? While they do these things, he says, expect them to grow, not decline. Then he gives the monks their own version. So here are two voices inside the tradition, each at its best. The first: keep the old ways. Not abolishing what was laid down is right there on the list. Tradition says that after the Buddha's death, the elders at the first council couldn't agree which small rules might be dropped, so they kept them all, and a shared form has held communities together ever since. The second: the same sutta records the Buddha saying that after he's gone, the sangha may set aside the lesser and minor rules if it wishes. He left room. A community that can't adapt can lose the people it's meant to serve. Teachers and schools still weigh these differently. But notice what comes first on the list, before any question of old or new: meet often, and meet in harmony. Disagree in the room. Leave it together.
screen: `DO THEY MEET OFTEN?` · `IN HARMONY, RISING IN HARMONY.` · `KEEP IT ALL, OR LEAVE ROOM?` · `FIRST: KEEP MEETING.` · then, large: `MEET IN HARMONY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one gathering you belong to, or could: a team, a class, a temple, a dinner table. Picture the next time it meets. Picture yourself there, arriving on time, listening to the person you usually disagree with, and leaving on good terms.
Community: in the Buddha's words to Ananda, people who meet often, meet in harmony, and rise together.
For your pocket: meet in harmony, even when you don't agree. Five of six on friends and community.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastic communities meet regularly, including the uposatha observance days, and lay communities gather at temples and centers for practice, festivals and decisions.

fork.setup: your temple's youth group wants to move the old festival to a weekend so more friends can come. the elders object. state the elders' best case.
options: old people just dislike change; there's nothing more to it.
a shared form handed down holds people together; keeping it is part of the harmony.
the festival belongs to the elders, so the youth should simply obey.
fork.reveal: that's the 'keep it all' voice at its best: not abolishing what was laid down is one of the conditions. the other voice can point to the Buddha leaving room.

original.note: Pali: united, in harmony; the word for how the Vajjis meet and rise.

trapdoor: what you thought: a community lasts if everyone agrees.
what it means: a community lasts if people keep meeting, and meet and part in harmony, even when they disagree.

what a scholar hears: DN 16 opens with the Vajjis' conditions of non-decline, then applies them to the sangha; its permission to drop minor rules, and the first council's choice to keep all, is told in the Vinaya's Cullavagga.

a group that agrees on everything and never argues
whoever happens to live in the same town as you
recall: next door is where all beings starts

chat.says: ông's temple meeting got LOUD. half want the new year festival the old way, half want changes. who's right?
options: Maybe both have a point. The Buddha's test: do they keep meeting, and part in harmony?
The old way. The Buddha said never change anything once it's been decided.
The new way. The Buddha said rules should change whenever people want.
chat.meaning: DN 16 holds both: keep what was laid down, and room to drop minor rules. What comes first is meeting often and in harmony.

tie.story: The Buddha said the Vajjis would thrive while they kept meeting, and met and rose in harmony.
tie.friend: Mai can tell Ông the fight matters less than everyone still showing up next month.
tie.you: which group of yours needs you to keep showing up?

Vajjis.meaning: a confederation of clans the Buddha praised for meeting in harmony

sangha.meaning: the community of monks and nuns, and more widely all who practice

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta: Vassakara's visit; the Vajjis' conditions of non-decline: meeting often, meeting and rising in harmony, keeping established ways, honoring elders; the same applied to the monks; permission to abolish the lesser and minor rules)
Vinaya, Cullavagga XI (the first council: the elders cannot agree which rules are minor and keep them all)

notes: DN 16 paraphrased; the conditions are given in part (protecting women, honoring shrines and protecting arahants left out for length). Confirm the paraphrase. 'In the last journey of the Buddha's life' frames DN 16; confirm.

Debate: 'keep it all' (not abolishing what was laid down; the first council's choice in Cullavagga XI) versus 'leave room' (the permission in DN 16 to set aside lesser and minor rules). 'A shared form has held communities together ever since' is interpretive; confirm. 'Teachers and schools still weigh these differently' is general and ranks none.
